abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for understanding cross-modal perceptual binding in augmented reality environments, fundamentally shifting how we conceptualize the integration of visual and haptic cues in spatially-anchored displays. Current models of human perception treat sensory channels as largely independent processors, failing to capture the dynamic recalibration that occurs when users interact with virtual objects overlaid on physical surfaces. We propose the Adaptive Sensory Calibration (ASC) theory, which posits that perceptual coherence emerges from a bidirectional weighting mechanism where visual dominance gradually yields to haptic confirmation as interaction time increases. Through rigorous psychophysical experiments involving 48 participants interacting with mixed-reality objects across varying spatial configurations, we demonstrate that this recalibration follows a predictable temporal trajectory characterized by distinct phases of initial dominance, conflict resolution, and stable fusion. The ASC framework successfully predicts perceptual judgment errors with 34% greater accuracy than existing integration models. This paradigm shift reconceptualizes applied perception as an active negotiation process rather than passive signal combination, offering profound implications for the design of perceptual user interfaces and the development of more intuitive augmented reality systems.

We present a substantially refined computational model for predicting visual conspicuity in complex virtual environments, addressing critical limitations in existing saliency-based approaches for computer graphics applications. Previous perceptual modeling efforts have demonstrated that standard bottom-up saliency metrics fail to account for task-dependent attention modulation, resulting in prediction accuracies that plateau below acceptable thresholds for practical deployment. Our enhanced Hierarchical Attention Distribution (HAD) model integrates domain-specific task priming, depth-guided visual search strategies, and temporal prediction mechanisms into a unified probabilistic framework. Evaluation across three independent benchmark datasets comprising 2,847 eye-tracking samples from virtual scene exploration tasks demonstrates that HAD reduces prediction error by 27.3% compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. The model's hierarchical structure enables graceful degradation in the presence of incomplete input information, a common occurrence in dynamic virtual reality scenarios. This work advances computational perception by providing graphics developers with a validated tool for predicting user attention distribution, facilitating evidence-based design decisions in immersive environment development.

We present HaptoSim, a groundbreaking perceptual evaluation system that fundamentally transforms how haptic feedback quality is assessed in human-computer interaction contexts. Existing evaluation methodologies rely on subjective user ratings or simplified performance metrics, providing limited insight into the underlying perceptual dimensions that drive haptic experience quality. HaptoSim introduces a dual-interface architecture combining a high-fidelity haptic rendering engine with an integrated psychophysical measurement subsystem capable of conducting adaptive threshold assessments in real-time. The system implements a novel stimulus generation paradigm using parameterized haptic textures that systematically vary along dimensions of roughness, compliance, and thermal conductivity. We demonstrate the system's utility through deployment in a comprehensive evaluation study involving 64 participants rating haptic feedback quality across 18 virtual surface categories. Results reveal previously unidentified perceptual clustering patterns suggesting that users process haptic quality through three distinct cognitive channels rather than as a unified percept. This paradigm innovation enables objective, quantifiable haptic quality assessment, providing researchers and developers with unprecedented tools for evidence-based design of perceptual user interfaces and haptic systems.

We describe a significantly enhanced perceptual user interface for gaze-contingent rendering in immersive virtual reality, achieving substantial improvements in visual quality preservation while reducing computational overhead. Previous approaches to foveated rendering have struggled with edge artifacts, noticeable transition zones, and inadequate adaptation to individual viewing patterns, limiting practical deployment in demanding VR applications. Our system introduces a biomimetic gaze prediction module trained on extensive oculomotor data from 89 users performing naturalistic exploration tasks, combined with a multi-resolution rendering pipeline featuring novel temporal smoothing that eliminates perceptual discontinuities during rapid eye movements. The interface achieves a 68% reduction in rendered pixel count while maintaining visually lossless perception in the central 5-degree field, validated through two-alternative forced choice experiments demonstrating that users cannot distinguish our rendered output from full-resolution reference with statistical significance. The system operates within strict latency constraints suitable for clinical-grade VR applications, completing all computations within 4.2 milliseconds on consumer hardware. This improved design enables practical deployment of high-fidelity VR experiences on resource-constrained platforms while preserving the perceptual richness essential for effective virtual reality applications.
